paragraphs: It was the beginning of November. There had been a hard frost, eleven degrees Réaumur, with no snow. But a little dry snow had fallen on the frozen ground during the night, and a keen, dry wind was lifting it and blowing it along the dreary streets of our town, especially around the market-place. It was a dull morning, but the snow had stopped.

Not far from the market-place, close to Plotnikov’s shop, stood a small house, very clean both inside and out. It belonged to Madame Krassotkin, the widow of a former provincial secretary, who had been dead for fourteen years. His widow, still a nice-looking woman of thirty-two, lived in her neat little house on her private means. She lived in respectable seclusion and had a soft but fairly cheerful disposition. She had been about eighteen when her husband died; she had been married only a year and had just borne him a son. From the day of his death she had devoted herself heart and soul to bringing up her precious treasure, her boy Kolya. She had loved him passionately for those fourteen years, but he had caused her far more suffering than happiness. Almost every day she trembled and nearly fainted with terror, afraid he would fall ill, catch cold, do something naughty, climb on a chair and fall off it, and so on and so on. When Kolya began going to school, his mother threw herself into studying all the sciences with him, to help him and go over his lessons with him. She hurried to get to know the teachers and their wives. She even made up to Kolya’s schoolfellows and fawned on them, hoping in this way to save Kolya from being teased, laughed at or beaten by them. She went so far that the boys actually began to mock him on her account and taunt him as a “mother’s darling.”

But the boy could stand up for himself. He was a resolute boy, “tremendously strong,” as was rumored in his class, and he soon proved it true. He was agile, strong-willed, and daring and enterprising. He was good at lessons, and there was a rumor in the school that he could beat the teacher, Dardanelov, at arithmetic and universal history. Though he looked down on everyone, he was a good comrade and not stuck-up. He took his schoolfellows’ respect as his due, but was friendly with them. Above all, he knew where to draw the line. He could restrain himself when he needed to, and with the teachers he never overstepped that last mystic limit beyond which a prank becomes an unpardonable breach of discipline. But he was as fond of mischief on every possible occasion as the smallest boy in the school, and not so much for mischief’s sake as for creating a sensation, inventing something, something effective and conspicuous. He was extremely vain. He knew how to make even his mother give way to him; he was almost despotic in his control of her. She gave way to him—oh, she had given way to him for years. The one thought she could not bear was that her boy did not love her very much. She was always imagining that Kolya was “unfeeling” toward her, and at times she would dissolve into hysterical tears and reproach him for his coldness. The boy disliked this, and the more displays of feeling were demanded of him, the more he seemed to avoid them on purpose. Yet it was not on purpose but by instinct—it was his character. His mother was mistaken; he was very fond of her. He only disliked “sheepish sentimentality,” as he put it in his schoolboy language.

There was a bookcase in the house with a few books that had been his father’s. Kolya liked reading and had read several of them by himself. His mother did not mind that. She only wondered sometimes to see the boy stand for hours by the bookcase, poring over a book instead of going out to play. In that way Kolya read some things unsuitable for his age.

Though the boy, as a rule, knew where to draw the line in his mischief, lately he had begun to play pranks that caused his mother serious alarm. There was nothing vicious in what he did, it is true, but there was a wild, mad recklessness.

It happened that July, during the summer holidays, that the mother and son went to another district, forty-five miles away, to spend a week with a distant relation whose husband was an official at the railway station (the very station, the nearest one to our town, from which a month later Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov set off for Moscow). There Kolya began by carefully studying every detail of the railways, knowing he could impress his schoolfellows with his newly acquired knowledge when he got home. But there happened to be some other boys in the place, and he soon made friends with them. Some of them lived at the station, others nearby; there were six or seven of them, all between twelve and fifteen, and two of them came from our town. The boys played together, and on the fourth or fifth day of Kolya’s stay at the station, the foolish boys made a mad bet. Kolya was almost the youngest of the group and was somewhat looked down on by the others for that. Moved by vanity or reckless bravado, he bet them two roubles that he would lie down between the rails at night when the eleven o’clock train was due, and lie there without moving while the train rolled over him at full speed. They did make a preliminary investigation, it is true, and it appeared that a person could lie so flat between the rails that the train would pass over without touching him. But to lie there was no joke! Kolya stoutly maintained that he would. At first they laughed at him and called him a little liar and a braggart, but that only egged him on. What stung him most was that these boys of fifteen turned up their noses at him so haughtily, and had at first been inclined to treat him as “a small boy,” not fit to associate with them. That was an unendurable insult.

And so it was decided to go in the evening, half a mile from the station, so that the train would have time to reach full speed after leaving it. The boys gathered. It was a pitch-dark night, with no moon. At the appointed time, Kolya lay down between the rails. The five others who had taken the bet waited among the bushes below the embankment. Their hearts beat with suspense, which was followed by alarm and remorse. At last they heard in the distance the rumble of the train leaving the station. Two red lights gleamed out of the darkness; the monster roared as it approached.

“Run, run away from the rails,” the boys cried to Kolya from the bushes, breathless with terror. But it was too late: the train darted up and flew past. The boys rushed to Kolya. He lay without moving. They began pulling at him and lifting him up. He suddenly got up and walked away without a word. Afterward he explained that he had lain there as though unconscious, to frighten them, but the fact was that he had really lost consciousness, as he confessed to his mother long after. That was how his reputation as “a desperate character” was established forever. He went back to the station as white as a sheet. Next day he had a slight attack of nervous fever, but he was in high spirits and well pleased with himself. The incident did not become known at once, but when they came back to town it made its way into the school and even reached the ears of the masters. But then Kolya’s mother hurried to plead with the masters on her boy’s behalf, and in the end Dardanelov, a respected and influential teacher, took up his cause, and the affair was ignored.

Dardanelov was a middle-aged bachelor who had been passionately in love with Madame Krassotkin for many years. About a year earlier he had already ventured once, trembling with fear and delicacy of feeling, to offer her his hand in marriage, most respectfully. But she had refused him flatly, feeling that to accept would be a betrayal of her son. Yet Dardanelov had reason, judging by certain mysterious signs, to believe that he was not disliked by the charming but too chaste and tender-hearted widow. Kolya’s mad prank seemed to have broken the ice, and Dardanelov was rewarded for his intercession with a hint of hope. The hint, it is true, was a faint one, but Dardanelov was such a paragon of purity and delicacy that it was enough, for the time being, to make him perfectly happy. He was fond of the boy, though he would have thought it beneath him to try to win him over, and he was severe and strict with him in class. Kolya, too, kept him at a respectful distance. He learned his lessons perfectly; he was second in his class, and he was reserved with Dardanelov, and the whole class firmly believed that Kolya was so good at universal history that he could “beat” even Dardanelov. Kolya had in fact asked him the question, “Who founded Troy?” and Dardanelov had given a very vague reply, referring to the movements and migrations of races, to the remoteness of the period, to the mythical legends. But the question “Who had founded Troy?”—that is, what individuals—he could not answer, and for some reason he even thought the question idle and frivolous. But the boys remained convinced that Dardanelov did not know who founded Troy. Kolya had read about the founders of Troy in Smaragdov, whose history was among the books in his father’s bookcase. In the end all the boys became interested in the question of who had founded Troy, but Krassotkin would not tell his secret, and his reputation for knowledge remained unshaken.

After the incident on the railway, a certain change came over Kolya’s attitude to his mother. When Anna Fyodorovna (Madame Krassotkin) heard of her son’s exploit, she almost lost her mind with horror. She had such terrible attacks of hysterics, lasting with intervals for several days, that Kolya, seriously alarmed at last, promised on his honor that such pranks would never be repeated. At Madame Krassotkin’s insistence he swore on his knees before the holy image, and swore by the memory of his father, and the “manly” Kolya burst into tears like a boy of six. And all that day mother and son kept rushing into each other’s arms, sobbing. Next day Kolya woke up as “unfeeling” as before, but he had become quieter, more modest, sterner and more thoughtful.

Six weeks later, it is true, he got into another scrape, which even brought his name to the ears of our Justice of the Peace. But it was a scrape of quite another kind, amusing and foolish, and as it turned out he did not take the leading part in it but was only implicated. But of this later. His mother still fretted and trembled, but the more uneasy she became, the greater grew Dardanelov’s hopes. It must be noted that Kolya understood and guessed what was in Dardanelov’s heart and, of course, despised him profoundly for his “feelings.” In the past he had been so tactless as to show this contempt before his mother, hinting vaguely that he knew what Dardanelov was after. But from the time of the railway incident his behavior in this respect also changed; he did not allow himself the slightest allusion to the subject, and he began to speak more respectfully of Dardanelov before his mother. The sensitive woman noticed this at once, with boundless gratitude. But at the slightest mention of Dardanelov by a visitor in Kolya’s presence, she would flush as pink as a rose. At such moments Kolya would either stare out of the window, scowling, or inspect the state of his boots, or shout angrily for “Perezvon,” the big, shaggy, mangy dog that he had picked up a month before, brought home, and kept indoors in secret for some reason, not showing him to any of his schoolfellows. He bullied the dog frightfully, teaching him all sorts of tricks, so that the poor dog howled for him whenever he was away at school, and when he came in, whined with delight, rushed about as if he were crazy, begged, lay down on the ground pretending to be dead, and so on. In fact he showed all the tricks he had been taught, not on command, but simply out of the zeal of his excited and grateful heart.

I have forgotten, by the way, to mention that Kolya Krassotkin was the boy who was stabbed with a penknife by the boy the reader already knows as the son of Captain Snegiryov. Ilusha had been defending his father when the schoolboys jeered at him and shouted the nickname “wisp of tow.”
